seoDescription: Learn the fundamentals of hand laminating a carbon fiber part using the accessible wet layup and vacuum bagging process. This tutorial guides you through every step, starting with preparing an offset mold using release wax. You'll see how to cut carbon fiber fabric, mix EL2 laminating resin, and apply multiple plies for a strong laminate. The video demonstrates two vacuum bagging methods: one using professional vacuum pumps and regulators, and an alternative using a household vacuum cleaner for great results on a budget.

summary:
## Core Process: Wet Layup & Vacuum Bagging

This video details how to create a carbon fiber part using the **hand lamination** (wet layup) method, consolidated with **vacuum bagging**. This process is more accessible than resin infusion or pre-pregs and can yield excellent results.

## Step 1: Mold Preparation

- **Release Agent**: The tutorial uses a traditional **mold release wax**.
- **Application**: Apply a thin film in a circular motion, allow it to haze (10-15 mins), then buff to a high polish.
- **Coats**: Repeat this process at least **4-5 times** to build up a reliable release layer.

## Step 2: Material Preparation

- **Pre-cutting**: Preparation is key. Pre-cut all reinforcements and vacuum bag consumables before mixing resin.
- **Cutting Carbon Fiber**: For a straight edge, snip the fabric and pull out a single tow to create a cutting guideline.

> [!TIP]
> While any sharp scissors work, dedicated **composite shears** make cutting easier and last longer.

- **Vacuum Bag**: For small parts, an **envelope bag** is easiest. Use sealant tape to seal the edges, being careful to avoid creases which cause leaks.

## Step 3: Mixing and Lamination

- **Resin Calculation**: For a wet layup, you need resin equal to the **weight of the fabric**, plus a small extra amount for waste.
- **Mixing**: Mix the resin and hardener thoroughly, scraping the sides and bottom. Pour into a second cup and mix again (**double-potting**) to ensure no unmixed components remain.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Accuracy in the mix ratio and thorough mixing are crucial for the epoxy to cure correctly.

- **Lamination Technique**: 
  1.  Apply a thin coat of resin to the mold first.
  2.  Carefully place the first (cosmetic) layer of carbon fiber, working from the center outwards.
  3.  Use a brush to **stipple** (press and dab) the fabric, driving the resin from underneath up through the fibers. Avoid brushing strokes, which can distort the weave.
  4.  Repeat for all subsequent layers.

## Step 4: Vacuum Bagging

- **Material Stack**: A simple, reliable stackup consists of:
  1.  **Peel Ply**: Placed directly on the wet laminate. It allows air/resin to pass through and provides a clean, bondable surface after being peeled off.
  2.  **Breather Cloth**: Placed over the peel ply. It creates an air path for the vacuum and absorbs excess resin.

### Professional Method

- **Equipment**: Uses a **vacuum pump and regulator**.
- **Pressure**: A **low vacuum level of around 20%** is ideal for this material stack to avoid pulling too much resin out of the laminate.
- **Cure**: The part is kept under vacuum for ~6 hours for the initial cure.

### DIY Alternative Method

- **Equipment**: Uses readily available **vacuum storage bags** (for clothes) and a **household vacuum cleaner**.
- **Pressure**: A typical household vacuum cleaner naturally pulls around the ideal **20% vacuum**.
- **Result**: This inexpensive method produces results that are nearly indistinguishable from those made with professional equipment, making it a great entry point.

## Results & Final Takeaways

- **Quality**: The wet layup and vacuum bag process can produce a near-perfect part, though minor **pinholes** can be expected. For a completely void-free finish, resin infusion would be necessary.
- **Versatility**: Wet layup allows for the use of a wide variety of reinforcement fabrics, including decorative carbon hybrids and dramatic spread-tow weaves.
transcription:
## Introduction to Wet Layup & Mold Preparation

Hi, I'm Paul from Easy Composites and today we're going to be using the offset mold that we made in a previous tutorial to produce this carbon fiber frame protector. In many of our recent videos, we've been using fairly advanced processes such as pre-pregs or resin infusion. But today, we're going to be looking at the much more accessible wet layup and vacuum bag process. I'll be showing you how to prepare the mold and the materials and then demonstrate the carbon fiber laminating itself before moving on to two alternative methods of vacuum bagging.

Although you may notice that we normally use the easy chemical release agent for room temperature applications, the more traditional mold release wax is a perfectly viable option. So today, that's what we're going to be using. And this small pot is included in the mold making starter kit. So to apply the wax, you just rub it in a circular motion as a thin film all over the surface of the mold. You then need to leave that to haze off, which will take 10 to 15 minutes, and then just gently buff the surface back down to get it back up to a full polish. And then that process then needs repeating at least four or five times to ensure that you're going to get a good, even thick film of wax over the surface.

## Materials & Equipment for the Project

Let's take a look at the materials we're going to be using. For a small project like this, our laminating starter kit is a really convenient package that includes the carbon fiber, the resin, some mixing ancillaries, gloves, and brushes.

## Vacuum Bagging Consumables & Tools

If you were just doing a normal wet layup, that's pretty much all of the material you would need. But as we will be going on to vacuum bag this project, we've also got the vacuum bagging consumables. So, we've got a breather, a peel ply, and a vacuum bagging film. The equipment we've got is a vacuum pump and regulator. And then we've also got a set of digital scales for weighing out the resin and some composite shears for cutting all of the materials.

Also, later on in this tutorial, we'll be demonstrating how the same vacuum bagging process can be undertaken using just a household vacuum cleaner and readily available vacuum compression bags.

With wet layup, the key to success really is in the preparation. So, we're going to be pre-cutting all of our reinforcements and preparing the vacuum bag to ensure that the layup process goes as smoothly as possible without any time pressure.

The laminating kit includes a small roll of our most popular 210 g 2x2 twill carbon fiber cloth. We carry this and many other reinforcements on our website.

In order to make a straight cut, the edge of the fabric can be snipped and a single tow pulled out. This then leaves you with a guideline to cut down.

Carbon fabrics can be cut with any good quality pair of scissors or shears. If you're working with composite reinforcements frequently, it would be worthwhile investing in some dedicated composite shears, which will make lighter work and last longer than conventional scissors.

## Creating the Vacuum Bag Envelope

The next thing to be prepared is the vacuum bag. This is cut a reasonable amount bigger than the part to ensure that there is sufficient film to follow the contours. For smaller parts, it's usually easier to make an envelope bag rather than trying to seal to the mold flanges. Vacuum bagging sealant tape is applied and all but one face is pre-sealed. Take great care not to get creases in the vacuum bag over the sealant tape as this will lead to a leak.

The through bag connector is now installed in a location that won't contact the surface of the part. And a piece of breather is placed beneath this to provide an air pathway to the part.

## Mixing the Laminating Resin

With all of the materials prepared, we're now ready to mix the resin. We're using the resin that comes in the starter kit, which is the EL2 laminating resin and the fast hardener.

For a wet layup, the amount of resin that you will need will be approximately the same weight of the amount of fabric that you have, plus a little extra that will be wasted in the pot and the brush.

As with all epoxies, the mix ratio should be followed as accurately as possible. When mixing the epoxy, this should be done thoroughly and steadily to avoid mixing in too much air. Ensure the sides and the bottom of the container are also scraped into the mix. It's common practice to pour this mix into a second cup and then mix again. This is to ensure that there is no unmixed resin trapped in the corner or against the sides of the pot.

## Laminating the First Layer of Carbon Fiber

So, the first step in a wet layup process is to apply a coat of resin onto the surface of the mold. The purpose of this is that the resin actually drives up through the fabric rather than trying to wet the fabric out from the back. This reduces the amount of air that you're likely to get trapped on the surface.

We're brushing on quite a thin coat because actually the first layer of reinforcement doesn't need that much resin. In fact, it would only need around about 200 g per square meter.

The first layer of reinforcement that goes into your mold is the most important. This is the cosmetic layer that you will see. And it's quite easy to get these loose strands of fiber underneath your fabric and that of course will lead to a cosmetic imperfection. So ensuring that the underside is clear, just gently place this centrally onto the mold.

And then just very gently working from the center, tack it down onto the resin.

So with the reinforcement in position, we're going to take a brush without too much resin on it and then stipple the surface. So, this is sort of pressing and consolidating the resin from underneath up through the fiber to the top.

It's important not to use sort of brush strokes in this situation because that's likely to disturb the weave and move it around. And if you're working on a larger part, a squeegee or a roller might help in this process. But something small like this, they're really not that practical. So, we're just going to use a brush and continue with this sort of stippling squeegee type action.

## Applying Subsequent Carbon Fiber Layers

With the first ply laminated, we're now ready to apply some more resin and then repeat the process for the second layer.

So again, it's just a thin thin coat, just enough to wet the next layer of reinforcement out.

Now with the second ply, just repeating the same process. So, tack it down from the center, work outwards, tacking it into place, and then just with a brush with no additional resin on, again, just sort of stippling or sort of squeegeeing the surface to drive it down.

We now have the first two plies laminated. The next two plies are just a repeat of the same process.

## Preparing the Laminate for Vacuum Bagging

If you were just doing a standard wet layup without vacuum bagging, this is the point where you would leave it to cure at room temperature. And with proper technique, excellent results can still be achieved this way. However, we're going to be going a step further and we're going to vacuum bag this part.

There are many possible combinations of vacuum bagging materials that can be used. However, we have found that a very simple stack of a peel ply followed by a breather used in conjunction with a low vacuum level provides very reliable results. The peel ply is laid down onto the back of the laminate in a similar way to carbon. The purpose of peel ply is to provide a membrane that will allow air and resin to pass through into the breather layer, but can later be peeled back from the cured laminate. It also has the benefit of leaving a very neat surface finish that is perfect for bonding to. The next layer into the mold is a breather cloth. This provides the air path for the air to escape under vacuum and also plays the role of absorbing any excess resin from the laminate. This is simply draped over the surface.

## Vacuum Bagging with Professional Equipment

This stack can now be placed and sealed into the vacuum bag that we made earlier and connected to the vacuum.

As the vacuum is pulling down, the bag should be manipulated into all of the contours and corners to avoid any bridging and ensure that an even pressure is applied over the entire part. With this stack of materials, the best results will be achieved with a low vacuum level of around 20%. Which is controlled using a vacuum regulator. If you don't have a regulator and only have high vacuum available, you would normally include a perforated release film between the peel ply and the breather to prevent drying out the laminate too far.

## Demolding and Inspecting the Cured Part

We'll keep this under vacuum for around 6 hours whilst the resin reaches its initial cure, at which stage the vacuum can be switched off and the part allowed to cure fully before demolding.

Having left this to fully cure, we can now remove it from the bag and demold it.

Now need to remove the peel ply and the breather. The peel ply tears away and breaks away from the surface. But as the breather has quite a lot of resin soaked into it, it will make it that little bit more difficult.

Although at first glance this part does look pretty much perfect, if you inspect it very closely, there are one or two spots where there's some small pin holes. Now, this is about as good as you can get from a wet laid and vacuum bag process. If you wanted a completely void-free surface, the resin infusion process will deliver that. We do have plenty of videos covering that subject, but overall I'm pretty happy with this. If you did want to flat this down and put a clear coat, any small imperfections like this would disappear.

## Alternative Method: Vacuum Bagging with a Household Vacuum

We've been using our professional-grade vacuum pump and regulator. And if you're working with composites every day, this sort of equipment is absolutely appropriate. However, we understand that not everybody has access to this equipment, especially if you're just starting out. So, it's perfectly possible to still achieve excellent results on small projects like this using vacuum storage bags. Now, these are the bags that are designed for compressing clothes for easy storage. Readily available online or from your local supermarket. Very often, they're included with a hand vacuum pump. Now, we've tested this pump and it actually achieves 80% vacuum, which is surprisingly high and too high for the project we're doing now. So, we also tested domestic vacuum cleaners and we found that generally they do achieve the ideal 20% vacuum.

## Applying the Alternative Method & Comparing Results

So, here we have another part laminated in just the same way as the first. You can't see it now, but we've used carbon Kevlar hybrid instead of the regular carbon fiber. As before, we seal it into the bag and pull a vacuum, but this time using a vacuum cleaner and relying on the valve and seal of the bag to hold the vacuum whilst this part reaches a full cure.

As you can see, using this method, we've still achieved a very good surface finish with only a few minor pin holes. And if we were to compare this method using the vacuum cleaner with the part we made earlier on using professional equipment, you'll notice that the results are almost indistinguishable, making this an inexpensive way to get started producing higher quality composite parts.

## Conclusion & Exploring Other Fabric Options

The first part that we produced was made using the 210 g 2x2 Twill carbon. Now, this is our most popular reinforcement and also the one that's included in the laminating starter kit. The second part that we made using the vacuum cleaner method was produced using a carbon kevlar hybrid. The great thing about the wet layup process is it opens up the possibility to use almost any reinforcement at all. So, we've got some examples here. We've got a decorative blue carbon hybrid and also a very dramatic looking carbon fiber spread tow here. This, of course, is only a very small selection of the reinforcements that you could use. So, if you go over to the Easy Composites website, you'll see our entire range that we have in stock.

I hope you've enjoyed this video. As ever, we always appreciate a like and a subscribe. And a special thank you goes out to all of our customers whose support makes these videos possible.
